screens.title: Hybrid Cloud Connectivity: VPN and Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: Extending an on-premises data center to AWS is a practical requirement for many enterprises. In this lesson you will understand the two primary connection models AWS offers: encrypted internet-based tunnels using Site-to-Site and Client VPN, and dedicated private links using Direct Connect. You will learn when each is appropriate, how routing and redundancy change the configuration, and what operational trade-offs to expect in bandwidth, latency, and cost. For example, a development lab often uses Site-to-Site VPN for quick setup and encrypted connectivity, while a production application with strict latency and bandwidth needs typically uses Direct Connect with private virtual interfaces. We will also step through a hands-on CLI demo to create a Virtual Private Gateway, Customer Gateway, and a Site-to-Site VPN, and explore a best-practice architecture that combines Direct Connect with a VPN fallback. By the end you will be able to evaluate requirements, choose an approach, and design for resilience. Consider which application in your environment needs predictable latency and which can tolerate internet-based variability — that distinction will guide your choice between VPN and Direct Connect.

Hybrid Cloud Connectivity: VPN and Direct Connect

Learn when to use encrypted internet tunnels, when to order dedicated private links, and how routing and redundancy differ between these approaches.

Why this matters
Hybrid connectivity controls performance, security, and cost for enterprise workloads moving across environments.
What you'll do
Evaluate VPN vs Direct Connect, configure a Site-to-Site VPN, and design Direct Connect with VIFs and gateway routing.
Visual preview
Concept map
Site-to-Site VPN

Direct Connect

Client VPN
Managed client access for remote users, integrates with Active Directory or certificates.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate AWS VPN and Direct Connect and select the correct option for an application. You will configure Site-to-Site VPN connections using either static or dynamic routing and understand how redundant tunnels work. You will also design Direct Connect virtual interfaces to access private VPC addresses or public AWS services, and use a Direct Connect Gateway to centralize connectivity across accounts and regions. Each of these objectives ties to a practical capability: choosing the right connectivity reduces latency and cost; configuring routing correctly avoids asymmetric paths; and using Direct Connect Gateway simplifies multi-account architectures. As a concrete example, you'll learn to set up a VGW attached to a VPC, create a Customer Gateway that represents an on-prem router, and establish a Site-to-Site VPN using BGP so routes flow dynamically. A common misconception is that VPN always equals low cost and Direct Connect always equals better security; the real trade-offs involve bandwidth, predictability, and whether you need a private network path. These objectives prepare you to make those distinctions and to verify connectivity in production.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are intentionally practical. First, when you evaluate VPN solutions, you'll consider bandwidth caps per tunnel and the need for two tunnels for redundancy. For example, Site-to-Site VPN tunnels commonly support up to about 1.25 gigabits per second per tunnel, and multiple tunnels or parallel connections can increase aggregate throughput. Second, understanding Direct Connect means knowing the difference between dedicated and hosted links and when to order a 10 gigabit port versus a hosted 200 megabit link through a partner. Third, configuring Site-to-Site VPN teaches you routing mechanics: static routes require manual updates, while BGP exchanges routes dynamically and simplifies failover. Fourth, designing Direct Connect with VIFs and a Direct Connect Gateway helps you centralize access to many VPCs across accounts and regions. In practice you will also verify failover by simulating a connection loss and ensuring traffic shifts to a VPN backup. A common mistake is assuming BGP removes the need to check firewall rules; always verify security groups and NACLs in addition to routing. These outcomes ensure you can both plan and operate hybrid connectivity reliably.

screens.title: What is hybrid cloud connectivity?
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid cloud connectivity refers to the network arrangements that let on-premises resources communicate with AWS resources. At its core this is about extending private networks so applications and data can move between environments while preserving security and performance. A useful analogy is a business that has two offices connected by either a secure leased line or the public postal service: Direct Connect is like a leased fiber link that you control and can rely on for predictable delivery, while VPN over the internet is like sending locked parcels via the public postal system — secure in transit but subject to variable delivery time. Practically, hybrid connectivity enables data migration, burst capacity to the cloud, disaster recovery, and phased application rehosting. A common misconception is that any connection labeled ‘VPN’ is automatically adequate for production; in reality you must assess bandwidth needs, latency sensitivity, and tolerance for jitter. For example, backups and telemetry can often tolerate VPN variability, but real-time transaction systems frequently need Direct Connect to meet SLAs. The takeaway: define the workload profile first, then choose the connectivity option that meets its performance and security needs.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Hybrid connectivity is the set of network choices and configurations that join on-premises networks to AWS with appropriate security and performance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is hybrid cloud connectivity?
Definition and analogy

Hybrid cloud connectivity lets on-premises networks and cloud VPCs communicate securely and reliably. The analogy: Direct Connect is a leased private line, Site-to-Site VPN is secure parcels sent over public mail.

When to use which
Match Direct Connect to workloads needing predictable latency; use VPN for quicker, cost-sensitive setups.
Common mistake
Assuming VPN is always ok for production without checking bandwidth and latency requirements.
Key Takeaway

Start with workload needs: bandwidth, latency, and security determine whether VPN or Direct Connect is the right choice.

Illustrative cards
Office example
Real-time trading systems use leased lines; developer laptops use VPN to reach cloud resources.
Operational benefit
Direct Connect lowers egress costs for heavy data flows and provides more predictable performance.
Misconception
Dedicated links eliminate the need for security controls — you still must enforce IAM, security groups, and NACLs.

screens.title: AWS Site-to-Site VPN: components and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates encrypted IPsec tunnels across the public internet to connect your on-premises router or firewall to an AWS Virtual Private Gateway or Transit Gateway. The essential components are the Customer Gateway, which represents your on-prem device and its public IP; the Virtual Private Gateway which is the AWS endpoint attached to a VPC; and the Site-to-Site VPN connection which includes two independent tunnels for redundancy, each with a separate AWS public IP. When you create a VPN you choose static routing or dynamic routing using BGP. Dynamic routing requires your on-premises device to support BGP, enabling automatic route exchange and faster failover. Static routes require manual updates on both sides when networks change. A concrete example: you create a VGW attached to a VPC, create a Customer Gateway with your router's public IP and ASN, then create a VPN connection with BGP enabled so route prefixes flow automatically. A common mistake is forgetting to update the VPC route table to point on-premises CIDRs at the VGW or forgetting NACL rules; both will prevent traffic even when a tunnel is up. The takeaway: configure both tunnel redundancy and routing correctly, and verify both tunnel status and route propagation.

keyIdea.title: Site-to-Site essentials
keyIdea.text: Two tunnels for redundancy, CGW and VGW endpoints, and BGP for dynamic route exchange are the core design elements.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Site-to-Site VPN: components and behavior
Process: Create and operate a Site-to-Site VPN
1. Create a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)
Attach it to the VPC that hosts your private resources.
2. Create a Customer Gateway (CGW)
Specify the public IP and BGP ASN of your on-prem router.
3. Create VPN connection with two tunnels
Choose dynamic BGP for automatic route exchange or static routes for manual control.
Example
A corporate router with ASN 65000 peers with AWS using BGP; when an on-prem subnet is added, it is advertised to AWS automatically.
Common mistake
Not updating the VPC route table to include the on-prem CIDR; the tunnel can be UP but traffic still fails.
Visual: component cards
Customer Gateway (CGW)
Represents the on-prem device and public IP; includes BGP ASN for dynamic routing.
Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)
AWS endpoint attached to a single VPC; receives VPN tunnels.
Tunnels and redundancy
Two tunnels with separate public IPs provide resilience. If one fails, traffic shifts to the other.

screens.title: AWS Client VPN
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Client VPN is a managed, client-based VPN service designed for remote users who need secure access to AWS resources or on-premises networks. It uses an OpenVPN-compatible client and can integrate with Active Directory or certificate-based authentication, giving you granular access control for users and groups. Client VPN is particularly useful for employees, contractors, or developers who must reach private management consoles, development environments, or test databases without exposing those systems directly to the internet. For example, a developer working from home can use Client VPN to securely access resources in a VPC as if they were on the corporate network. A common misconception is treating Client VPN as a substitute for Site-to-Site VPN; instead, it complements Site-to-Site by serving user access rather than site connectivity. Operationally, plan how Client VPN subnet associations, route configurations, and authorization rules map to your VPC subnets. Also, ensure you configure logging and rotation of certificates or credential stores. The key takeaway: use Client VPN to provide secure, managed, and auditable remote access for users while keeping site-to-site tunnels for permanent on-premises networks. AWS Client VPN means a managed remote-access vpn using openvpn clients, integrated with directory or certificate authentication for user-level access.. In practical terms, secure remote access for users and developers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › AWS Client VPN
What it is and when to use it

Client VPN grants remote users secure access to VPC resources and on-prem networks using a managed OpenVPN service. It supports directory and certificate authentication and provides authorization rules per subnet.

Concrete example
A remote engineer uses Client VPN to access a private build server in a VPC without exposing the server to the internet.
Design note
Plan subnet associations and route propagation so users can reach required subnets and resources.
Misconception
Client VPN is for user access, not for permanent site-to-site connectivity — don't replace CGW/VGW with Client VPN for datacenter links.
Operational checklist
Authentication
Integrate with Active Directory or certificate stores to control user access.
Authorization rules
Define which VPC CIDRs and subnets users can access and log connections for auditing.
Key Takeaway

Use Client VPN for user-level secure access; maintain separate Site-to-Site tunnels for persistent datacenter connectivity.

screens.title: AWS Direct Connect: types and benefits
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Direct Connect provides a private network link between your premises and AWS, bypassing the public internet. The two common procurement options are Dedicated Connections and Hosted Connections. A Dedicated Connection gives you a physical port ordered directly from AWS and is available in high speeds such as 1, 10, or 100 gigabits per second. A Hosted Connection is provisioned through an AWS Direct Connect partner and typically offers smaller increments like 50, 100, or 500 megabits per second up to 10 gigabits. The practical benefits include lower network egress costs for large data transfers, more consistent latency and throughput, and enhanced security because traffic does not traverse the internet. For example, if your application requires sustained transfers of multiple terabytes per day and low jitter, a Dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect is usually the right choice. A common trap is ordering insufficient capacity or not planning redundant paths; for high availability you should provision diverse Direct Connect locations or combine Direct Connect with a Site-to-Site VPN fallback. The core insight: Direct Connect is about predictability and cost control at scale — order the type and size that match sustained throughput needs and design redundancy into the path.

keyIdea.title: Direct Connect benefits
keyIdea.text: Direct Connect delivers predictable bandwidth, potentially lower costs for large transfers, and a private path suited to latency-sensitive workloads.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › AWS Direct Connect: types and benefits
Dedicated vs Hosted

Dedicated connections are physical ports ordered from AWS with large bandwidth options. Hosted connections come through partners and offer smaller increments suitable for organizations that do not need a full port.

When to choose Direct Connect
When predictable performance, lower egress for high volume, and private connectivity are required.
Design tip
Plan redundancy across Direct Connect locations or provide a VPN backup for connectivity resilience.
Key Takeaway

Select Dedicated for sustained high throughput and Hosted for incremental capacity through partners; always plan path diversity.

Visual: speed and use cases
Speeds
Common Dedicated: 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps. Hosted: 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps through partners.
Use cases
Large data migration, database replication, video ingest, and latency-sensitive transactions.

screens.title: Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) and Direct Connect Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: After establishing a Direct Connect connection you create Virtual Interfaces — logical links that carry traffic over the physical connection. There are two primary VIF types: Private and Public. A Private VIF connects to a Virtual Private Gateway or Direct Connect Gateway and is used to access resources in your VPCs using private IP addresses. A Public VIF lets you reach AWS public endpoints such as S3 or public EC2 IPs over the private Direct Connect link instead of traversing the internet. When you need to connect a single Direct Connect to multiple VPCs across accounts or regions, a Direct Connect Gateway is the central resource that maps the Direct Connect to multiple Virtual Private Gateways. For example, an enterprise with multiple AWS accounts can provision a single Direct Connect and use a Direct Connect Gateway to present connectivity to VGWs in each account, simplifying management and avoiding separate direct links for each VPC. A common operational step is to attach a Private VIF to a Direct Connect Gateway and then associate that gateway with VGWs in target accounts. Be mindful of route propagation and BGP: you will typically use BGP for dynamic route exchange across VIFs. The takeaway: VIFs and Direct Connect Gateway let you scale private connectivity and simplify cross-account access when designed with routing in mind.

keyIdea.title: VIF and Gateway
keyIdea.text: Private VIFs reach VPC private IPs; Public VIFs reach public AWS endpoints; Direct Connect Gateway enables multi-VPC, multi-account connectivity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › VIFs and Direct Connect Gateway
VIF types and purpose
Private VIFs connect to your VPCs through VGW or Direct Connect Gateway to carry private IP traffic. Public VIFs carry traffic to public AWS services over the private link.
Private VIF
Used for VPC private IP traffic; attach to Direct Connect Gateway for multi-VPC reachability.
Public VIF
Used to access AWS public endpoints like S3 without traversing the internet.
Key Takeaway

Use Direct Connect Gateway to scale a single connection across multiple VGWs and accounts while managing routes via BGP.

Scenario card
Enterprise example
A single Direct Connect with a Private VIF attached to a Direct Connect Gateway serves VGWs in multiple accounts for centralized connectivity.
Operational note
Ensure ASNs and BGP sessions are correctly configured so routes propagate from on-prem to each VGW through the Direct Connect Gateway.

screens.title: VPN vs Direct Connect: trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect requires looking at four dimensions: bandwidth, latency consistency, security posture, and cost. Bandwidth: VPN tunnels typically provide up to about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel, and higher aggregate throughput can be achieved with multiple tunnels or VPN endpoints, but Direct Connect offers dedicated ports from 50 Mbps up to 100 Gbps depending on the connection type. Latency and consistency: Direct Connect bypasses the public internet which reduces jitter and provides a predictable path; VPN traverses the internet and can exhibit variable latency. Security posture: both can provide encrypted connectivity, but Direct Connect’s private path reduces exposure to public internet transit. Cost: for large sustained data transfer Direct Connect can lower egress costs and be more economical despite port fees. A practical example: choose Site-to-Site VPN for a temporary migration tunnel or development environment, and choose Direct Connect for production databases that replicate continuously across sites. Misconception check: Direct Connect is not inherently a replacement for VPN redundancy — combining Direct Connect with a VPN fallback is a common pattern to ensure full availability. The key takeaway is to weigh workload needs and design redundancy accordingly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › VPN vs Direct Connect: trade-offs
Side-by-side comparison
VPN
Encrypted over internet, fast to set up, two tunnels for redundancy, up to ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel.
Direct Connect
Private dedicated link with fixed bandwidth options and lower variability; available as Dedicated or Hosted.
Latency
VPN: variable. Direct Connect: consistent and lower jitter.
Cost
VPN: lower setup cost. Direct Connect: port fees but potential egress savings at scale.
Misconception
Direct Connect removes security responsibility — you still must control access with IAM, security groups, and network rules.
Scenario guidance
Low-cost, moderate bandwidth
Use Site-to-Site VPN for development, proof-of-concept, and modest production traffic.
High-performance, private
Use Direct Connect with Private VIF and Direct Connect Gateway to centralize multi-VPC access.
Key Takeaway

Match the choice to workload needs and combine both for redundancy when necessary.

screens.title: Designing redundancy: best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Designing hybrid connectivity for high availability requires layered redundancy. For Site-to-Site VPN the first level of resilience is the pair of tunnels AWS provisions for a VPN connection; each tunnel has a different public IP and endpoint. You should also consider multiple VPN connections or multiple CGWs to distribute risk. For Direct Connect, redundancy often means provisioning connections to separate Direct Connect locations, using diverse physical paths or working with a partner that provides path diversity. A practical architecture pattern is to make Direct Connect the primary path for production traffic and configure a Site-to-Site VPN as an automatic fallback. In that design you rely on BGP for dynamic route failover: when the Direct Connect path withdraws routes, the VPN BGP session advertises alternative paths so traffic shifts. A common pitfall is relying on DNS or manual changes for failover; you want BGP to handle route changes automatically. Also test your failover procedures: simulate an outage on the primary path and verify route withdrawal and re-advertisement behave as expected. The takeaway: design multiple, diverse paths and verify them with realistic failure tests to ensure connectivity when it matters.

You should also consider multiple VPN connections or multiple CGWs to distribute risk. For Direct Connect, redundancy often means provisioning connections to separate Direct Connect locations, using diverse physical paths or working with a partner that provides path diversity. A practical architecture pattern is to make Direct Connect the primary path for production traffic and configure a Site-to-Site VPN as an automatic fallback. In that design you rely on BGP for dynamic route failover: when the Direct Connect path withdraws routes, the VPN BGP session advertises alternative paths so traffic shifts. A common pitfall is relying on DNS or manual changes for failover; you want BGP to handle route changes automatically. Also test your failover procedures: simulate an outage on the primary path and verify route withdrawal and re-advertisement behave as expected. The takeaway: design multiple, diverse paths and verify them with realistic failure tests to ensure connectivity when it matters.

Two VPN tunnels per connection for intra-connection redundancy.
Multiple Direct Connect connections at diverse locations for path diversity.
Design Direct Connect primary with Site-to-Site VPN fallback and use BGP for automatic route failover.
Test plan
Simulate primary link loss and confirm BGP route withdrawal triggers VPN path advertisement and traffic shift.

Diversity and automation (BGP) are the foundations of robust hybrid connectivity; verify with realistic tests.

Failure scenarios
Single tunnel loss
Traffic remains on the second tunnel without manual intervention.
Direct Connect outage
BGP withdraws routes; VPN advertises alternate routes and traffic migrates to the internet-based tunnel.

screens.title: Hands-on CLI: create a VGW, CGW, and Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: In this walkthrough you'll see the AWS CLI commands to create a Virtual Private Gateway, attach it to a VPC, create a Customer Gateway representing your on-prem router, and then create a Site-to-Site VPN that uses BGP. Execute these commands from an environment with AWS CLI configured. First create the VGW and attach it to your VPC; this prepares the AWS endpoint. Next create the Customer Gateway and provide your on-prem public IP and ASN; this declares the other side of the tunnel. Then create the VPN connection and request dynamic routing so BGP is used. After creation, download the vendor-specific configuration or query the VPN connection attributes to see tunnel endpoints and pre-shared keys. In practice you would apply the configuration to your physical router: program the IPsec tunnels and configure BGP peering using the provided ASN and neighbor addresses. Finally update your VPC route table to send on-premises CIDRs via the VGW and verify the tunnel states using the describe command. A common error is not updating the route table or forgetting firewall rules — always confirm routing and packet flow after the tunnel is UP. Now review the sample CLI commands shown in the code panel and use them as a starter template for your lab.

keyIdea.text: Use aws ec2 commands to create a VGW, CGW, and VPN connection; download config and verify tunnel status and route tables.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › CLI: Create VGW, CGW, VPN
Starter commands (example)
Use these aws ec2 commands as a template. Replace IDs and IPs with your environment values.
# 1. Create a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)
aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway --type ipsec.1 --amazon-side-asn 64512

# Attach VGW to VPC
aws ec2 attach-vpn-gateway --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0a1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8 --vpc-id vpc-1234567890abcdef0

# 2. Create a Customer Gateway (CGW)
aws ec2 create-customer-gateway --type ipsec.1 --public-ip <ON_PREM_PUBLIC_IP> --bgp-asn 65000

# 3. Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection with BGP
aws ec2 create-vpn-connection \
  --type ipsec.1 \
  --customer-gateway-id cgw-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0a1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8 \
  --options '{"StaticRoutesOnly":false}'

# 4. Verify VPN connection and tunnel status
aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections --vpn-connection-ids vpn-0fedcba9876543210
Apply the downloaded config
Use the vendor configuration to program IPsec parameters, pre-shared keys, and BGP neighbors on your router.
Verification and checks
Route tables
Add routes for on-prem CIDRs to the VPC route table pointing to the VGW.
Tunnel status
Confirm both tunnels are UP; check configuration if either is down.
Firewall rules
Ensure NACLs and firewalls allow traffic between on-prem and VPC subnets; NACLs are stateless so allow both directions.

screens.title: Common connectivity issues and diagnostics
screens.narratorSegment: When users report connectivity problems across a VPN or Direct Connect link there are a few diagnostic steps to follow. First, check tunnel state: both Site-to-Site VPN tunnels should show UP in the console or via the describe command. If a tunnel is down inspect IPsec parameters, pre-shared keys, and the network path from your router to AWS public IPs. Second, verify routing: ensure the VPC route table contains entries for on-prem CIDRs pointing to the VGW, and that your on-prem router advertises the VPC CIDRs via BGP or static routes. Asymmetric routing is a frequent cause of failures — traffic leaving AWS toward on-prem may take a different path back if routes or NAT are misconfigured. Third, check security controls: security groups are stateful but NACLs are stateless, so both inbound and outbound rules must allow the traffic. Finally, inspect BGP ASNs and neighbor states: mismatched ASNs or missing BGP neighbors will prevent route exchange. A concrete troubleshooting sequence: confirm tunnel UP, check VPC route table, verify on-prem route advertisement, and review NACLs and firewall logs. The takeaway: verify both the tunnel and route plane as well as network ACLs to find the root cause.

Diagnostic checklist
1. Tunnel status
Confirm both tunnels are UP; if down, inspect IPsec config, keys, and network reachability.
2. Routing
Check VPC route tables and on-prem route advertisements; ensure correct CIDRs and next-hops are configured.
3. BGP and ASNs

A systematic check of tunnel state, routing, and security rules quickly reveals most hybrid connectivity issues.

Scenario example
Symptom
Tunnel shows UP but instances cannot be reached from on-prem.
Diagnosis steps
1) Check VPC route table for route to on-prem; 2) Confirm on-prem advertises VPC CIDR; 3) Inspect NACLs and security groups.
Prevention
Document routing maps and test failover scenarios regularly to catch misconfigurations early.

screens.title: Simulated lab: configure and verify a Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: This simulated lab walks you through the practical steps of establishing a Site-to-Site VPN and verifying its operation. Begin by creating a Virtual Private Gateway and attaching it to your VPC. Next create a Customer Gateway by specifying the public IP and ASN of your on-prem router. Create the VPN connection with dynamic routing so BGP handles route exchange. Download the vendor-specific configuration and apply it to your router, programming both IPsec tunnels and configuring BGP neighbors with the provided ASNs and peer addresses. Update the VPC route table to include the on-prem CIDR with the VGW as the target. For verification, use the describe-vpn-connections command to confirm both tunnels are UP and check that BGP routes are present in the VPC route propagation. If traffic does not flow, confirm NACLs allow both directions, security groups permit the necessary ports, and that your on-prem router is advertising the correct VPC CIDRs. In this simulated environment, you should see the VPN state as available, tunnels report UP, and routes propagate automatically via BGP. The takeaway: follow the checklist precisely and validate both the tunnel and routing plane to ensure connectivity.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the central ideas to retain. Hybrid Cloud means combining on-premises infrastructure with cloud resources. Site-to-Site VPN creates IPsec tunnels over the internet with two tunnels for redundancy and supports static or BGP routing. Customer Gateway represents your on-prem device, and Virtual Private Gateway is the AWS endpoint attached to a VPC. AWS Client VPN is for remote user access and integrates with authentication stores. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these compact definitions close as you design hybrid networks. fullNarratorScript:
Extending an on-premises data center to AWS is a practical requirement for many enterprises. In this lesson you will understand the two primary connection models AWS offers: encrypted internet-based tunnels using Site-to-Site and Client VPN, and dedicated private links using Direct Connect. You will learn when each is appropriate, how routing and redundancy change the configuration, and what operational trade-offs to expect in bandwidth, latency, and cost. For example, a development lab often uses Site-to-Site VPN for quick setup and encrypted connectivity, while a production application with strict latency and bandwidth needs typically uses Direct Connect with private virtual interfaces. We will also step through a hands-on CLI demo to create a Virtual Private Gateway, Customer Gateway, and a Site-to-Site VPN, and explore a best-practice architecture that combines Direct Connect with a VPN fallback. By the end you will be able to evaluate requirements, choose an approach, and design for resilience. Consider which application in your environment needs predictable latency and which can tolerate internet-based variability — that distinction will guide your choice between VPN and Direct Connect.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate AWS VPN and Direct Connect and select the correct option for an application. You will configure Site-to-Site VPN connections using either static or dynamic routing and understand how redundant tunnels work. You will also design Direct Connect virtual interfaces to access private VPC addresses or public AWS services, and use a Direct Connect Gateway to centralize connectivity across accounts and regions. Each of these objectives ties to a practical capability: choosing the right connectivity reduces latency and cost; configuring routing correctly avoids asymmetric paths; and using Direct Connect Gateway simplifies multi-account architectures. As a concrete example, you'll learn to set up a VGW attached to a VPC, create a Customer Gateway that represents an on-prem router, and establish a Site-to-Site VPN using BGP so routes flow dynamically. A common misconception is that VPN always equals low cost and Direct Connect always equals better security; the real trade-offs involve bandwidth, predictability, and whether you need a private network path. These objectives prepare you to make those distinctions and to verify connectivity in production.

These objectives are intentionally practical. First, when you evaluate VPN solutions, you'll consider bandwidth caps per tunnel and the need for two tunnels for redundancy. For example, Site-to-Site VPN tunnels commonly support up to about 1.25 gigabits per second per tunnel, and multiple tunnels or parallel connections can increase aggregate throughput. Second, understanding Direct Connect means knowing the difference between dedicated and hosted links and when to order a 10 gigabit port versus a hosted 200 megabit link through a partner. Third, configuring Site-to-Site VPN teaches you routing mechanics: static routes require manual updates, while BGP exchanges routes dynamically and simplifies failover. Fourth, designing Direct Connect with VIFs and a Direct Connect Gateway helps you centralize access to many VPCs across accounts and regions. In practice you will also verify failover by simulating a connection loss and ensuring traffic shifts to a VPN backup. A common mistake is assuming BGP removes the need to check firewall rules; always verify security groups and NACLs in addition to routing. These outcomes ensure you can both plan and operate hybrid connectivity reliably.

Hybrid cloud connectivity refers to the network arrangements that let on-premises resources communicate with AWS resources. At its core this is about extending private networks so applications and data can move between environments while preserving security and performance. A useful analogy is a business that has two offices connected by either a secure leased line or the public postal service: Direct Connect is like a leased fiber link that you control and can rely on for predictable delivery, while VPN over the internet is like sending locked parcels via the public postal system — secure in transit but subject to variable delivery time. Practically, hybrid connectivity enables data migration, burst capacity to the cloud, disaster recovery, and phased application rehosting. A common misconception is that any connection labeled ‘VPN’ is automatically adequate for production; in reality you must assess bandwidth needs, latency sensitivity, and tolerance for jitter. For example, backups and telemetry can often tolerate VPN variability, but real-time transaction systems frequently need Direct Connect to meet SLAs. The takeaway: define the workload profile first, then choose the connectivity option that meets its performance and security needs.

AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates encrypted IPsec tunnels across the public internet to connect your on-premises router or firewall to an AWS Virtual Private Gateway or Transit Gateway. The essential components are the Customer Gateway, which represents your on-prem device and its public IP; the Virtual Private Gateway which is the AWS endpoint attached to a VPC; and the Site-to-Site VPN connection which includes two independent tunnels for redundancy, each with a separate AWS public IP. When you create a VPN you choose static routing or dynamic routing using BGP. Dynamic routing requires your on-premises device to support BGP, enabling automatic route exchange and faster failover. Static routes require manual updates on both sides when networks change. A concrete example: you create a VGW attached to a VPC, create a Customer Gateway with your router's public IP and ASN, then create a VPN connection with BGP enabled so route prefixes flow automatically. A common mistake is forgetting to update the VPC route table to point on-premises CIDRs at the VGW or forgetting NACL rules; both will prevent traffic even when a tunnel is up. The takeaway: configure both tunnel redundancy and routing correctly, and verify both tunnel status and route propagation.

AWS Client VPN is a managed, client-based VPN service designed for remote users who need secure access to AWS resources or on-premises networks. It uses an OpenVPN-compatible client and can integrate with Active Directory or certificate-based authentication, giving you granular access control for users and groups. Client VPN is particularly useful for employees, contractors, or developers who must reach private management consoles, development environments, or test databases without exposing those systems directly to the internet. For example, a developer working from home can use Client VPN to securely access resources in a VPC as if they were on the corporate network. A common misconception is treating Client VPN as a substitute for Site-to-Site VPN; instead, it complements Site-to-Site by serving user access rather than site connectivity. Operationally, plan how Client VPN subnet associations, route configurations, and authorization rules map to your VPC subnets. Also, ensure you configure logging and rotation of certificates or credential stores. The key takeaway: use Client VPN to provide secure, managed, and auditable remote access for users while keeping site-to-site tunnels for permanent on-premises networks. AWS Client VPN means a managed remote-access vpn using openvpn clients, integrated with directory or certificate authentication for user-level access.. In practical terms, secure remote access for users and developers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Direct Connect provides a private network link between your premises and AWS, bypassing the public internet. The two common procurement options are Dedicated Connections and Hosted Connections. A Dedicated Connection gives you a physical port ordered directly from AWS and is available in high speeds such as 1, 10, or 100 gigabits per second. A Hosted Connection is provisioned through an AWS Direct Connect partner and typically offers smaller increments like 50, 100, or 500 megabits per second up to 10 gigabits. The practical benefits include lower network egress costs for large data transfers, more consistent latency and throughput, and enhanced security because traffic does not traverse the internet. For example, if your application requires sustained transfers of multiple terabytes per day and low jitter, a Dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect is usually the right choice. A common trap is ordering insufficient capacity or not planning redundant paths; for high availability you should provision diverse Direct Connect locations or combine Direct Connect with a Site-to-Site VPN fallback. The core insight: Direct Connect is about predictability and cost control at scale — order the type and size that match sustained throughput needs and design redundancy into the path.

After establishing a Direct Connect connection you create Virtual Interfaces — logical links that carry traffic over the physical connection. There are two primary VIF types: Private and Public. A Private VIF connects to a Virtual Private Gateway or Direct Connect Gateway and is used to access resources in your VPCs using private IP addresses. A Public VIF lets you reach AWS public endpoints such as S3 or public EC2 IPs over the private Direct Connect link instead of traversing the internet. When you need to connect a single Direct Connect to multiple VPCs across accounts or regions, a Direct Connect Gateway is the central resource that maps the Direct Connect to multiple Virtual Private Gateways. For example, an enterprise with multiple AWS accounts can provision a single Direct Connect and use a Direct Connect Gateway to present connectivity to VGWs in each account, simplifying management and avoiding separate direct links for each VPC. A common operational step is to attach a Private VIF to a Direct Connect Gateway and then associate that gateway with VGWs in target accounts. Be mindful of route propagation and BGP: you will typically use BGP for dynamic route exchange across VIFs. The takeaway: VIFs and Direct Connect Gateway let you scale private connectivity and simplify cross-account access when designed with routing in mind.

Comparing Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect requires looking at four dimensions: bandwidth, latency consistency, security posture, and cost. Bandwidth: VPN tunnels typically provide up to about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel, and higher aggregate throughput can be achieved with multiple tunnels or VPN endpoints, but Direct Connect offers dedicated ports from 50 Mbps up to 100 Gbps depending on the connection type. Latency and consistency: Direct Connect bypasses the public internet which reduces jitter and provides a predictable path; VPN traverses the internet and can exhibit variable latency. Security posture: both can provide encrypted connectivity, but Direct Connect’s private path reduces exposure to public internet transit. Cost: for large sustained data transfer Direct Connect can lower egress costs and be more economical despite port fees. A practical example: choose Site-to-Site VPN for a temporary migration tunnel or development environment, and choose Direct Connect for production databases that replicate continuously across sites. Misconception check: Direct Connect is not inherently a replacement for VPN redundancy — combining Direct Connect with a VPN fallback is a common pattern to ensure full availability. The key takeaway is to weigh workload needs and design redundancy accordingly.

Designing hybrid connectivity for high availability requires layered redundancy. For Site-to-Site VPN the first level of resilience is the pair of tunnels AWS provisions for a VPN connection; each tunnel has a different public IP and endpoint. You should also consider multiple VPN connections or multiple CGWs to distribute risk. For Direct Connect, redundancy often means provisioning connections to separate Direct Connect locations, using diverse physical paths or working with a partner that provides path diversity. The takeaway: design multiple, diverse paths and verify them with realistic failure tests to ensure connectivity when it matters.

Keep these compact definitions close as you design hybrid networks. Customer Gateway is your on-prem router or appliance that represents the local endpoint of a Site-to-Site VPN. Virtual Private Gateway is the AWS-side endpoint attached to a VPC that receives VPN tunnels. Virtual Interface is the logical link over Direct Connect and can be private to reach VPCs or public to reach AWS public services. BGP is the recommended dynamic routing protocol for automatic route exchange across Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN when supported, while static routing requires manual updates. Finally, Direct Connect Gateway lets a single Direct Connect serve multiple VGWs across accounts and regions, simplifying enterprise-scale connectivity. When you design connectivity, verify route advertisement and tunnel states, and plan for fallback paths. These concise definitions will help you quickly recall the right components and their purposes during architecture and operations.
